objectives: Distinguish parallel DDR from serial PCIe interfaces.

slides.title: From parallel buses to serial links
slides.body:
Historical interfaces: parallel (PCI 64-bit parallel, IDE 40-pin). Many wires, same clock. Slow per pin but wide.

Problem: at higher speeds, parallel buses suffer from **skew** (wires not arriving simultaneously) + **crosstalk** (signal interference between wires). Skew accumulates over distance.

Modern solution: **serial differential links** at very high frequency per pair. SerDes (Serializer-Deserializer).

**SerDes**: takes parallel data + serializes onto one or a few differential pairs at multi-Gbps. Receiver de-serializes back.

Advantages:
- Each pair gets clean signal integrity (differential rejects common-mode noise).
- Embedded clock (recovered from data, no separate clock distribution).
- Fewer pins (PCIe Gen5 x4 = 8 wires; PCIe Gen3 x32 = 64 wires for similar bandwidth).

**Modern speeds**:
- PCIe 4.0: 16 Gbps/lane.
- PCIe 5.0: 32 Gbps/lane.
- PCIe 6.0: 64 Gbps/lane (PAM-4 encoding).
- 100GbE: 25 Gbps × 4 lanes (NRZ) or 50 Gbps × 2 lanes (PAM-4).
- 400GbE: 50 Gbps × 8 lanes (PAM-4).
- Ethernet 1.6T (2024+): 200 Gbps × 8 lanes (PAM-4).

**SerDes building blocks**:
- **Transmitter**: parallel-to-serial conversion + line driver + pre-emphasis (boost high frequencies to compensate for channel loss).
- **Receiver**: CDR (Clock + Data Recovery — extract clock from data transitions), equalizer (compensate channel rolloff), serial-to-parallel.
- **Encoding**: 8b/10b (older, 20% overhead), 64b/66b (newer, 3% overhead), PAM-4 (4 voltage levels = 2 bits/symbol).

**Power**: SerDes dominate die power at high data rates. A single 112 Gbps SerDes consumes ~1 W. A switch chip with 256 SerDes burns 256 W on links alone.

slides.title: DDR + PCIe interfaces
slides.body:
**DDR (Double Data Rate) DRAM interfaces**: parallel but high-speed.
- DDR3: 800-2133 MT/s (mega transfers per second).
- DDR4: 2133-3200 MT/s.
- DDR5: 4800-8400 MT/s.
- LPDDR5X (mobile): up to 9600 MT/s.

Key features:
- 64-bit data bus + ECC bits.
- Source-synchronous clock (DQS strobes alongside data).
- Training: at power-up, controller + DRAM negotiate per-pin delays for optimal timing.
- Bank groups, prefetch buffers, on-die ECC.

DDR5 added on-die ECC (1-bit-per-byte correction) because cells are too small to be reliable without it.

**HBM (High Bandwidth Memory)**: TSV-stacked DRAM. 1024-bit bus per stack. 3.2 Gbps/pin → 3.2 TB/s per stack. Used in GPUs (HBM3 in NVIDIA H100 + AMD MI300).

**PCIe (Peripheral Component Interconnect Express)**: serial differential. 1-16 lanes per slot.
- Gen 3: 8 GT/s (gigatransfers/sec). x16 = 16 GB/s.
- Gen 4: 16 GT/s. x16 = 32 GB/s.
- Gen 5: 32 GT/s. x16 = 64 GB/s.
- Gen 6: 64 GT/s (PAM-4). x16 = 128 GB/s.

Layered architecture:
- Physical: SerDes, encoding.
- Data link: flow control, error correction.
- Transaction: packets to/from devices.

**CXL (Compute Express Link)**: built on PCIe physical layer. Adds cache coherence + memory pooling. CXL 1.1, 2.0, 3.0 progressively added features. Used in disaggregated memory + accelerator-CPU communication.

**Other interconnects**:
- **UCIe** (Universal Chiplet Interconnect): die-to-die in chiplet designs. Intel/AMD/TSMC backed.
- **InfiniBand**: HPC clusters. ~400 Gbps NDR latest.
- **NVLink**: NVIDIA proprietary, GPU-to-GPU. 900 GB/s per link in H100.
- **AMD Infinity Fabric**: similar for AMD.

slides.title: Network-on-Chip (NoC)
slides.body:
Modern SoCs have ~10-100+ cores + accelerators + memory controllers. Connecting them all via wires becomes infeasible at scale. **NoC**: packetized network INSIDE the chip.

**Architecture**:
- **Routers**: at each node. Switch packets between input + output ports.
- **Links**: wires connecting adjacent routers.
- **Network interfaces**: convert between core-protocol (cache requests) + NoC packets.

**Topologies**:
- **Bus**: single shared wire (legacy AMBA AHB / APB). Limited bandwidth.
- **Crossbar**: full crossbar between all sources + destinations. Wide bandwidth but doesn't scale.
- **Ring**: nodes in a circle. Used in Intel server chips (CCX ring).
- **Mesh / 2D-mesh**: grid of routers. Used in many many-core systems (Intel Xeon Sapphire Rapids, IBM Power).
- **Torus**: ring in both X + Y. Used in some HPC chips.
- **Hierarchical / tree**: clusters connected hierarchically. Used in some modern SoCs.

**Routing**:
- **Dimension-ordered (XY routing)**: first move in X, then Y. Deadlock-free.
- **Adaptive routing**: pick path based on congestion. More efficient but harder.

**Flow control**:
- **Store-and-forward**: receive entire packet, then forward.
- **Cut-through / wormhole**: start forwarding as head arrives. Lower latency.
- **Virtual channels**: multiple independent FIFOs per link. Prevents head-of-line blocking + helps deadlock avoidance.

**Cache-coherence over NoC**: a CPU read might need to invalidate other cores' caches. Hundreds of coherence messages per cycle in busy systems. The coherence protocol (MESI, MOESI) runs on top of the NoC.

**Examples**:
- **AMD Infinity Fabric**: scalable mesh + ring connecting CPU dies, GPU dies, I/O dies.
- **Apple UltraFusion**: connects two M-series chips into one via silicon interposer.
- **Tilera (Mellanox)**: 64-core mesh chips.
- **NVIDIA + Intel HBI / EMIB**: connects accelerator dies in package.

**Modern frontier**: chiplets. Multiple smaller dies in one package, connected by high-bandwidth NoC-like interfaces (UCIe, CXL). Improves yield + lets companies mix nodes (advanced 3nm compute + mature 7nm I/O).

question.question: Compute PCIe bandwidth for an SSD
question.goal: PCIe Gen 4 x4 NVMe SSD: 4 lanes × 16 GT/s. 128b/130b encoding overhead.

steps.prompt: 128b/130b encoding: 128 bits of data per 130 transmitted. Efficiency = 128/130 ≈ 0.985. Effective data rate?

steps.reveal: ~7.9 GB/s. Roughly matches the ~7 GB/s sustained throughput of high-end Gen4 NVMe SSDs (some overhead for protocol, sustained writes lower due to controller).

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{PCIe Gen N x M bandwidth} = N \times M \times \text{enc-eff}}$$ Modern systems: high-end GPUs use PCIe Gen5 x16 (64 GB/s). NVMe SSDs use Gen4 or Gen5 x4 (~8-15 GB/s). NICs use Gen5 x16 for 800 GbE. The bandwidth scaling has driven storage, networking, accelerator deployment. PCIe Gen6 (PAM-4 encoded) doubles again, deployed 2025+.

question.question: Why have parallel buses (DDR aside) largely been replaced by serial SerDes links in modern chips?
options: At high frequencies (>1 GHz), parallel buses suffer from skew + crosstalk + signal-integrity issues. Single high-speed differential pairs scale better, embed clock, use fewer pins.
question.explanation: Parallel bus problems at GHz speeds: (1) skew between wires (different delays); (2) crosstalk (capacitive + inductive coupling between adjacent wires); (3) clock distribution (a separate clock pin doesn't arrive in sync with data); (4) pin count. Serial differential links solve all: clock embedded in data (CDR recovers), differential rejects common-mode noise, fewer pins. Modern chip-to-chip interfaces (PCIe, CXL, USB, SATA, HDMI, DisplayPort) are all serial SerDes.

hints: What goes wrong with parallel at high frequency?
slides.workedSolution: Parallel: skew + crosstalk + clock-data sync all degrade above ~1 GHz. Serial differential pairs: clean signal (differential rejects noise), embedded clock (CDR), pin-efficient. Modern interconnects: PCIe, SATA, Ethernet, USB — all serial differential. Exception: DRAM (DDR) keeps parallel for legacy + cost; HBM uses high-pin-count parallel within package.

question.question: NVLink 4 (H100): 18 links × 25 GB/s. Total bandwidth per GPU?
Bottleneck in a many-core SoC
question.prompt: A 64-core SoC has a 2D-mesh NoC. Profiling reveals cache-coherence traffic causes hotspot congestion at the home-node directories. Walk through architectural options.
Explain in two or three sentences why interconnect design has become as important as core microarchitecture in modern processors.
question.rubric: Mentions that single cores have stopped scaling (frequency, IPC), so performance comes from MORE cores + accelerators; the interconnect determines effective bandwidth + latency between them; on-die NoC + chip-to-chip (PCIe / CXL / NVLink / UCIe) are the bottleneck for many workloads. The 'memory wall' + 'communication wall' increasingly dominate over compute.
